humanities_role_explanation: Targets disciplinary competence in art history, iconography, and aesthetic theory. Rather than treating artworks as raw data for generic visual QA, it structures evaluations around a 5-layer framework representing the ascending levels of art-historical interpretation (derived from Panofsky's iconological method and culture-specific concepts like yijing and rasa).
benchmark_modalities_explanation: Multimodal benchmark combining high-resolution images of cultural artworks with expert-annotated bilingual (English and Chinese) critiques.
analytical_tasks_explanation: Generative art-critique writing that spans five analytical layers: visual perception (L1), technical analysis of medium/brushwork (L2), decoding of cultural symbolism and iconography (L3), historical context and provenance/artist attribution (L4), and philosophical aesthetics/indigenous theory interpretation (L5).

general_purpose_benchmark.note: Specifically scoped to multicultural art history, visual arts critique, and cultural-philosophical interpretation.

evaluates_generative_llm.note: Evaluates several generative vision-language models including GPT-4o, Claude-Sonnet-4.5, Gemini-2.5-Pro, Qwen3-VL-235B, GLM-4V-Flash, and DeepSeek-VL2.

quantitative_metrics.note: Uses Dimension Coverage Rate (DCR) evaluated via keyword-matching, backed up by human ratings, open-source embedding models (BGE-large-en-v1.5), and NLI entailment.

summary: VULCA-BENCH is a multicultural, bilingual (Chinese-English) vision-language benchmark containing 7,410 image-critique pairs across eight cultural traditions. It introduces a hierarchical five-layer framework based on Panofsky's iconological method to systematically evaluate how well vision-language models can move from basic visual perception to complex historical and philosophical aesthetic analysis. The benchmark enforces cultural symmetry, ensuring minority aesthetic traditions are methodologically evaluated alongside Western art.
key_findings: Evaluated vision-language models show a steep performance drop of 31 to 40 percentage points when moving from lower-level visual perception (L1-L2) to higher-level cultural and philosophical interpretation (L3-L5). Furthermore, naive few-shot prompting actually degrades performance in several prominent models, emphasizing that simple in-context learning is insufficient to elicit deep cultural understanding.
facets_explanation: The reference critiques were written and reviewed by bilingual domain experts with PhDs or advanced training in art history and regional studies. Disagreements between annotators and reviewers were resolved through structured discussion and consensus to establish a singular gold-standard critique, thereby treating divergence as noise. Correctly evaluating the higher layers (L3–L5) requires external historical, cultural, and philosophical knowledge that cannot be extracted from the image stimulus alone.
results_explanation: The paper reports a performance gap between difficulty regimes (shallow L1–L2 vs. deep L3–L5 tiers of their taxonomy). In Table 7, 'all models show a 31–40 percentage-point drop', with the largest drop observed for 'GPT-4o' which falls from '87.1' on L1–L2 to '46.8' on L3–L5 (a gap of 40.3 percentage points, rounded to 40). The headline best overall score is '72.4' achieved by 'Gemini-2.5-Pro' on the primary metric 'Dimension Coverage Rate (DCR)' (Table 7). No quantified human baseline or expert reference score is reported on this same metric, so the human gap is null. Although the benchmark spans 8 cultural traditions, no systematic performance asymmetry across cultures is reported for the evaluated models.
